title: श्रीमद्भगवद्गीता — आत्मसंयमयोगः
titleEn: The Bhagavad Gītā — Chapter 6: The Yoga of Self-Restraint

अनाश्रितः कर्मफलं कार्यं कर्म करोति यः ।
स संन्यासी च योगी च न निरग्निर्न चाक्रियः ॥
sentences.tr:
anāśritaḥ karma-phalam kāryam karma karoti yaḥ |
saḥ saṃnyāsī ca yogī ca na niragniḥ na ca akriyaḥ ||

sentences.l: Not relying on the fruit of action, who does the action that is to be done — he is a renouncer and a yogin, not the fireless one, nor the actionless.
sentences.i: One who performs the action he is bound to do, without relying on its fruit, is both a renouncer and a yogin — not the man who has given up the sacred fires, and not the man who does nothing at all.
sentences.n: Kāryaṃ karma, 'the action that is to be done', is the obligatory or prescribed act — one's duty, as opposed to acts undertaken for private desire; the phrase recalls 2.47's teaching that one's entitlement is to the action itself. The verse redefines both saṃnyāsin, 'renouncer', and yogin as one and the same person, against two popular misconceptions: niragni, 'fireless', a man who has given up the Vedic sacrificial fires, and akriya, 'actionless', a man who does nothing at all — neither outward abstention makes the true renouncer. Sandhi: निरग्निर्न is niragniḥ + na; चाक्रियः is ca + akriyaḥ.

sentences.t:
यं संन्यासमिति प्राहुर्योगं तं विद्धि पाण्डव ।
न ह्यसंन्यस्तसंकल्पो योगी भवति कश्चन ॥
sentences.tr:
yam saṃnyāsam iti prāhuḥ yogam tam viddhi pāṇḍava |
na hi asaṃnyasta-saṃkalpaḥ yogī bhavati kaścana ||

renunciation (acc. sg., predicate complement: 'as renunciation')

sentences.l: Which they call renunciation, that know to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava; for no one who has not renounced his resolve becomes a yogin.
sentences.i: What they call renunciation, know that to be yoga as well, Pāṇḍava; for no one becomes a yogin without giving up his willed intentions.
sentences.n: Saṃkalpa is the willed intention behind an act — the "renunciation" meant is renunciation of that intention, not of action itself, a distinction the chapter develops concretely in verses 4 and 24-26. Sandhi: प्राहुर्योगं is prāhuḥ + yogam; ह्यसंन्यस्तसंकल्पो is hi + asaṃnyasta-saṃkalpaḥ. The verse identifies saṃnyāsa and yoga as a single thing, continuing 5.4-5's claim that sāṃkhya and yoga yield the same fruit.

sentences.t:
आरुरुक्षोर्मुनेर्योगं कर्म कारणमुच्यते ।
योगारूढस्य तस्यैव शमः कारणमुच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
ārurukṣoḥ muneḥ yogam karma kāraṇam ucyate |
yoga-ārūḍhasya tasya eva śamaḥ kāraṇam ucyate ||

morph.gloss: to climb, mount, ascend (ārurukṣu: desiderative adjective 'desiring to climb', gen. sg. 'of one desiring to ascend'; -oḥ + m- → -or m-)
a sage, contemplative (gen. sg., agreeing with ārurukṣoḥ; -eḥ + y- → -er y-)

to say (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is said, is called')

sentences.l: For one desiring to climb, a sage, to yoga, action is said to be the means; for him who has climbed to yoga, quiescence is said to be the means.
sentences.i: For the sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means; for one who has already ascended to yoga, stillness is said to be the means.
sentences.n: A mountaineering image: ārurukṣu, 'desiring to climb' (a desiderative form), against yogārūḍha, 'having climbed', mark the two stages of practice — action (karma) is the means while one is still climbing toward yoga, while quiescence (śama), the cessation of further striving, sustains one who has already attained it. This refines the equivalence of saṃnyāsa and yoga just claimed in verse 2 by placing them at different points on the same path. Sandhi: आरुरुक्षोर्मुनेर्योगं is ārurukṣoḥ + muneḥ + yogam, the visarga becoming r before the voiced m and then er before y-.

sentences.t:
यदा हि नेन्द्रियार्थेषु न कर्मस्वनुषज्जते ।
सर्वसंकल्पसंन्यासी योगारूढस्तदोच्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
yadā hi na indriya-artheṣu na karmasu anuṣajjate |
sarva-saṃkalpa-saṃnyāsī yoga-ārūḍhaḥ tadā ucyate ||

sentences.l: When indeed neither in the objects of the senses nor in actions he clings — one who has renounced all resolve, he is then called one who has attained yoga.
sentences.i: When a person no longer clings to the objects of the senses or to actions, having renounced all intention, he is then called one who has attained yoga.
sentences.n: This makes yogārūḍha, 'one who has ascended to yoga' (from verse 3), concrete: non-attachment both to sense-objects and to actions themselves, achieved by sarva-saṃkalpa-saṃnyāsa, 'renouncing all intention' — the very saṃkalpa named in verse 2. Sandhi: नेन्द्रियार्थेषु is na + indriya-artheṣu; कर्मस्वनुषज्जते is karmasu + anuṣajjate; योगारूढस्तदोच्यते packs three words, yoga-ārūḍhaḥ + tadā + ucyate.

sentences.t:
उद्धरेदात्मनात्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् ।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
sentences.tr:
uddharet ātmanā ātmānam na ātmānam avasādayet |
ātmā eva hi ātmanaḥ bandhuḥ ātmā eva ripuḥ ātmanaḥ ||

self (ātmānam: acc. sg., object of uddharet)

self (ātmā: nom. sg., subject)

sentences.l: Let one raise up the self by the self; let one not let the self sink down. For the self alone is the friend of the self, the self alone is the enemy of the self.
sentences.i: One should lift oneself up by one's own efforts, and never let oneself sink down; for the self alone is one's own friend, and the self alone is one's own enemy.
sentences.n: The verse turns on a deliberate double use of ātman — the self that must be raised, and the self that does the raising — resolved in the next verse: the self that has mastered itself becomes its own friend, an unmastered self its own enemy. Uddharet and avasādayet are both optatives of exhortation, 'let one'. Verses 5-6 open a short passage on self-mastery that leads into the meditation instructions beginning at verse 10.

बन्धुरात्मात्मनस्तस्य येनात्मैवात्मना जितः ।
अनात्मनस्तु शत्रुत्वे वर्तेतात्मैव शत्रुवत् ॥

anātmanaḥ tu śatrutve varteta ātmā eva śatru-vat ||

sentences.l: The self is the friend of the self of him by whom the self has been conquered by the self; but of him whose self is unconquered, in enmity the self alone would behave, like an enemy.
sentences.i: For a man who has conquered himself by himself, his own self is his friend; but for a man who has not mastered himself, his very self acts like an enemy, in open enmity.
sentences.n: This resolves verse 5's play on ātman: for one whose self has been "conquered" by himself, the self is a friend; for one lacking such mastery — anātman, literally "non-self", glossed by Śaṅkara as anātmavat, "one without self-mastery" — the self turns hostile, behaving like an actual enemy (śatru-vat). This completes the friend/enemy image and leads into the description of the self-conquered man that opens verse 7.

sentences.t:
जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः ।
शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः ॥

śīta-uṣṇa-sukha-duḥkheṣu tathā māna-apamānayoḥ ||

sentences.l: Of the self-conquered, the tranquil one, the supreme Self is settled — in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, likewise in honor and dishonor.
sentences.i: For the man who has conquered himself and grown tranquil, the supreme Self stands in steady composure — alike in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and in honor and dishonor.
sentences.n: Paramātmā samāhitaḥ: Śaṅkara reads this as "the supreme Self is [already] realized, settled" for such a man, who therefore abides unmoved regardless of external opposites; the same dvandva pairing as 2.14's śītoṣṇa-sukha-duḥkha is here extended to a third pair, honor and dishonor. The vulgate text translated here reads mānāpamānayoḥ, "in honor and dishonor" (apamāna, "insult, dishonor"); the BORI critical edition reads mānāvamānayoḥ (avamāna, a near-synonym also meaning "dishonor"), with no difference in sense.

sentences.t:
ज्ञानविज्ञानतृप्तात्मा कूटस्थो विजितेन्द्रियः ।
युक्त इत्युच्यते योगी समलोष्टाश्मकाञ्चनः ॥
sentences.tr:
jñāna-vijñāna-tṛpta-ātmā kūṭa-sthaḥ vijita-indriyaḥ |
yuktaḥ iti ucyate yogī sama-loṣṭa-aśma-kāñcanaḥ ||

equal, the same (first compound member)
a clod of earth (second member)
a stone (aśma-, third member; loṣṭa + aśma → loṣṭāśma)

sentences.l: Whose self is satisfied with knowledge and discernment, standing unmoved as on a peak, of conquered senses — "disciplined" he is called, the yogin, to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are alike.
sentences.i: A man whose mind is content with knowledge and its realization, who stands unmoved as if on a mountain peak, his senses mastered, and to whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are all the same — such a man is called a true yogin.
sentences.n: Jñāna and vijñāna are traditionally read, following Śaṅkara, as scriptural or theoretical knowledge and its personally realized counterpart; kūṭastha, "standing on a peak" (kūṭa can also mean "anvil", giving "immovable as an anvil"), pictures the same unshakeable steadiness developed in the lamp-simile of verse 19. Sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcanaḥ, "to whom a clod, a stone, and gold are the same", is the verse's concrete test of equal-sightedness — indifference to the very thing people prize most — and anticipates the equal vision extended to friend and foe in verse 9 and to all beings in verses 29-32.

साधुष्वपि च पापेषु समबुद्धिर्विशिष्यते ॥

suhṛt-mitra-ari-udāsīna-madhyastha-dveṣya-bandhuṣu |

a friend (second member; mitra + ari → mitrāri)
an enemy, foe (third member; ari + udāsīna → aryudāsīna, -i + u- → -y u-)

sentences.l: Toward well-wishers, friends, enemies, the indifferent, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen — even among the virtuous and the wicked, the one of equal mind excels.
sentences.i: The man who looks with an equal mind on well-wishers, friends and enemies, on the indifferent and the arbitrating, on the hateful and on his own kinsmen, and even on the virtuous and the wicked — he stands supreme.
sentences.n: One long compound fills the entire first line, naming seven kinds of person in the locative plural, all governed by sama-buddhiḥ, "of equal mind", in the second line: a well-wisher, a friend, an enemy, a neutral party, a mediator, someone hateful, and a kinsman. This equal-mindedness toward every kind of person, friend and foe alike, extends the sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcanaḥ of verse 8 and anticipates the sama-darśana, "equal vision", of verses 29-32; cf. also 2.38's counsel to hold pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as the same.

sentences.t:
योगी युञ्जीत सततमात्मानं रहसि स्थितः ।
एकाकी यतचित्तात्मा निराशीरपरिग्रहः ॥
sentences.tr:
yogī yuñjīta satatam ātmānam rahasi sthitaḥ |
ekākī yata-citta-ātmā nirāśīḥ aparigrahaḥ ||

to yoke, join, discipline (oneself) (yuñjīta: optative middle 3rd sg. 'should discipline, should yoke [his mind]')
constantly, always (adverb)
self (ātmānam: acc. sg., object of yuñjīta)
a secluded, solitary place (loc. sg. 'in solitude')

sentences.l: The yogin should constantly discipline the self, staying in solitude, alone, of restrained mind and self, without desire, without possessions.
sentences.i: The yogin should constantly discipline himself, staying alone in solitude, his mind and self restrained, free of desire and free of possessions.
sentences.n: This opens the meditation instructions that run through verse 32: solitude (rahasi), being alone (ekākī), restraint of mind (yata-citta), and freedom from both desire (nirāśīḥ) and possession (aparigrahaḥ) are named as the outward and inward conditions for practice, developed into specific posture instructions in verses 11-13.

to raise up (ucchrita: past participle 'raised, high'; ati-ucchrita: 'too high', acc. sg. neut., agreeing with āsanam; ati + u- → aty u-)
not (na + a- → nā-)
excessively (prefix)
low (ati-nīca: 'too low', acc. sg. neut.)
cloth (first compound member)
a deer- or antelope-skin (second member; caila + ajina → cailājina)
kuśa grass (third member)

placed above, laid over (kuśa-uttara: 'topped, one over the other'; caila-ajina-kuśa-uttaram: 'covered with kuśa-grass, hide, and cloth, layered one upon the other', acc. sg. neut., agreeing with āsanam; kuśa + uttara → kuśottara)

sentences.l: In a pure spot having established a firm seat for himself, not too high, not too low, covered with cloth, hide, and kuśa-grass —
sentences.i: Having set up a firm seat for himself in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, covered over with cloth, deerskin, and kuśa-grass in turn,
sentences.n: Verses 11-13 form one long sentence describing the yogin's seat and posture, completed by the verb in verse 12 (upaviśya ... yuñjyāt). Caila-ajina-kuśa-uttaram describes the traditional layered seat — kuśa grass spread on the ground, a deer- or antelope-skin over it, and a cloth on top — a construction still followed in classical yoga manuals. Nāty-ucchritaṃ nāti-nīcam, "neither too high nor too low", is a stock phrase for the moderate mean appropriate to a stable seat.

sentences.t:
तत्रैकाग्रं मनः कृत्वा यतचित्तेन्द्रियक्रियः ।
उपविश्यासने युञ्ज्याद्योगमात्मविशुद्धये ॥
sentences.tr:
tatra eka-agram manaḥ kṛtvā yata-citta-indriya-kriyaḥ |
upaviśya āsane yuñjyāt yogam ātma-viśuddhaye ||

morph.gloss: there, on that [seat] (tatra + e- → tatrai-)
one, single (first compound member)
point, tip (eka-agra: 'one-pointed', acc. sg. neut., agreeing with manaḥ)
mind (acc. sg. neut., object of kṛtvā)
to make (kṛtvā: gerund 'having made')
to restrain (yata: past participle, first compound member)
mind (second member)
sense-organ (third member; citta + indriya → cittendriya)
activity, function (yata-citta-indriya-kriyā: 'whose activities of mind and senses are restrained', nom. sg.)
to sit down (upaviśya: gerund 'having sat down')
seat (āsane: loc. sg. 'on the seat'; upaviśya + ā- → upaviśyā-)
to yoke, join, discipline (oneself) (yuñjyāt: optative 3rd sg. 'should practice'; -t + y- → -d y-)
yoga (acc. sg., object of yuñjyāt)
self (first compound member)
purification (ātma-viśuddhi: 'purification of the self', dat. sg. 'for the purification of the self'; yogam + ā- → yogamā-)

sentences.l: There, having made the mind one-pointed, of restrained activities of mind and senses, having sat down on the seat, let him practice yoga for the purification of the self.
sentences.i: There, having made the mind one-pointed and holding the activities of mind and senses in check, let him sit on that seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self.
sentences.n: This completes the sentence begun in verse 11: tatra, "there", refers back to the seat just described. Ekāgra, "one-pointed" (literally "having a single point"), is the technical term for concentrated attention used throughout later yoga literature. Ātma-viśuddhaye, "for the purification of the self", names the immediate purpose of the practice whose posture verse 13 goes on to describe.

sentences.t:
समं कायशिरोग्रीवं धारयन्नचलं स्थिरः ।
सम्प्रेक्ष्य नासिकाग्रं स्वं दिशश्चानवलोकयन् ॥
sentences.tr:
samam kāya-śiraḥ-grīvam dhārayan acalam sthiraḥ |
samprekṣya nāsikā-agram svam diśaḥ ca an-avalokayan ||

morph.gloss: even, level (acc. sg. neut., predicate agreeing with kāya-śiro-grīvam)
body, torso (first compound member)
head (second member; -aḥ before g- → -o)
neck (kāya-śiraḥ-grīvam: 'body, head, and neck', acc. sg. neut., object of dhārayan)
to hold, keep (causative dhārayan: present participle 'holding, keeping', nom. sg.; dhārayan + a- → dhārayanna-)
unmoving, motionless (acalam: acc. sg. neut., predicate)
firm, steady (nom. sg., agreeing with the implied subject 'he')
to gaze fixedly at (samprekṣya: gerund 'having gazed at, fixing his gaze on')
nose (first compound member)
tip (nāsikā-agra: 'the tip of the nose', acc. sg. neut., object of samprekṣya)
one's own (acc. sg. neut., agreeing with nāsikāgram)
direction, quarter (diśaḥ: acc. pl., object of avalokayan; -aḥ + c- → -aś c-)
and
not to look about, not to glance (causative avalokayan: present participle 'looking about, glancing'; an-avalokayan: 'not glancing about', nom. sg.; ca + a- → cā-)

sentences.l: Holding the body, head, and neck even, motionless, steady, gazing fixedly at the tip of his own nose, and not glancing about at the directions,
sentences.i: Holding body, head and neck erect and motionless, steady, fixing his gaze on the tip of his own nose, and not glancing about in any direction,
sentences.n: This continues the posture instruction of verses 11-12, completed by the main verb āsīta in verse 14. Kāya-śiro-grīvam samam, "body, head and neck even", describes the erect spine of classical seated meditation posture; the fixed gaze at the nose-tip and the injunction not to glance about both steady outward attention as a support for the inward stillness described next.

sentences.t:
प्रशान्तात्मा विगतभीर्ब्रह्मचारिव्रते स्थितः ।
मनः संयम्य मच्चित्तो युक्त आसीत मत्परः ॥
sentences.tr:
praśānta-ātmā vigata-bhīḥ brahmacāri-vrate sthitaḥ |
manaḥ saṃyamya mat-cittaḥ yuktaḥ āsīta mat-paraḥ ||

morph.gloss: to become fully calm (praśānta: past participle 'tranquil', first compound member)
self (praśānta-ātman: 'whose mind is tranquil', nom. sg.)
to depart (vigata: past participle 'departed, gone', first compound member)
fear (vigata-bhī: 'from whom fear has departed, fearless', nom. sg.; -īḥ + b- → -īr b-)
a celibate student, one observing chastity (first member)
a vow (brahmacāri-vrata: 'the vow of chastity', loc. sg. 'abiding in the vow of chastity')
to stand, abide (sthita: past participle 'abiding', nom. sg.)
mind (acc. sg., object of saṃyamya)
to restrain, control (saṃyamya: gerund 'having restrained')
me (stem form in compound)
mind (mat-citta: 'whose mind is fixed on me', nom. sg.; -aḥ before y- → -o)
to yoke, join, discipline (oneself) (yukta: past participle 'disciplined', nom. sg.; -aḥ dropped before the vowel ā-)
to sit, remain (āsīta: optative middle 3rd sg. 'let him sit, let him remain')
me (first compound member)
intent upon, devoted to (mat-para: 'devoted to me, with me as the highest', nom. sg.)

sentences.l: Of tranquil mind, fearless, abiding in the vow of chastity, having restrained the mind, his mind fixed on me, disciplined, let him sit, devoted to me.
sentences.i: Tranquil in mind, fearless, keeping to the vow of a celibate student, having restrained his mind and fixed it on me, let him sit, disciplined and devoted to me above all.
sentences.n: Brahmacāri-vrata, "the vow of the celibate student", names chastity as one requirement of the practice, alongside tranquility and fearlessness. Mac-cittaḥ ... mat-paraḥ, "mind on me ... devoted to me", is the first point in the meditation instructions where Kṛṣṇa names himself as the object of concentration, rather than the impersonal ekāgra, "one-pointed", of verse 12 — a personal focus resumed in verses 15, 30-31, and 47.

sentences.t:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी नियतमानसः ।
शान्तिं निर्वाणपरमां मत्संस्थामधिगच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
yuñjan evam sadā ātmānam yogī niyata-mānasaḥ |
śāntim nirvāṇa-paramām mat-saṃsthām adhigacchati ||

morph.gloss: to yoke, join, discipline (oneself) (yuñjan: present participle 'disciplining', nom. sg.; yuñjan + e- → yuñjanne-)
thus, in this way
always (sadā + ā- → sadā-)
self (ātmānam: acc. sg., object of yuñjan)
a yogin (nom. sg., subject)
to restrain, control (niyata: past participle 'restrained', first compound member)
mind (niyata-mānasa: 'of restrained mind', nom. sg.)
peace (acc. sg., object of adhigacchati)
extinction, cessation of passion (first compound member)
supreme (nirvāṇa-parama: 'culminating in liberation', acc. sg. fem., agreeing with śāntim)
me (stem form)
abiding in, resting in (mat-saṃsthā: 'having its resting-place in me', acc. sg. fem., agreeing with śāntim; saṃsthām + a- → saṃsthāma-)
to attain, reach (adhigacchati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Thus always disciplining the self, the yogin of restrained mind attains the peace that culminates in extinction of passion, that rests in me.
sentences.i: Thus always disciplining himself, the yogin of restrained mind attains the peace that culminates in liberation and has its resting-place in me.
sentences.n: This closes the posture-and-practice sequence begun at verse 11 with its result: śānti, "peace", qualified as nirvāṇa-paramā, "having extinction of passion as its highest point", and mat-saṃsthā, "abiding in me", tying the impersonal language of cessation to the personal devotion just introduced in verse 14. Nirvāṇa here, as at 5.24-26's brahma-nirvāṇam, denotes liberation, not the later Buddhist technical sense, though the word is shared.

sentences.t:
नात्यश्नतस्तु योगोऽस्ति न चैकान्तमनश्नतः ।
न चाति स्वप्नशीलस्य जाग्रतो नैव चार्जुन ॥
sentences.tr:
na ati-aśnataḥ tu yogaḥ asti na ca ekāntam anaśnataḥ |
na ca ati svapna-śīlasya jāgrataḥ na eva ca arjuna ||

to be (asti: present 3rd sg.)
not

not to eat (anaśnat: present participle 'not eating', gen. sg. 'for one who does not eat at all'; ekāntam + a- → ekāntama-)
not
and, nor (ca + a- → cā-)
excessively (prefix, continuing to modify svapna-śīlasya)
sleep (first compound member)

to be awake (jāgrat: present participle 'being awake', gen. sg. 'for one who stays awake'; -aḥ before n- → -o)
not (na + e- → nai-)

Arjuna (vocative)

sentences.l: Yoga is not for one who eats too much, nor indeed for one who does not eat at all, nor for one excessively given to sleep, nor indeed for one who stays always awake, Arjuna.
sentences.i: Yoga is not for the man who eats too much, nor for one who does not eat at all; not for one who sleeps too much, nor for one who stays always awake, Arjuna.
sentences.n: This turns from posture to regimen, ruling out extremes of both eating (atyaśnataḥ, anaśnataḥ) and sleep (svapna-śīlasya, jāgrataḥ) as incompatible with yoga — a moderation the next verse states positively, and which anticipates the critique of extreme asceticism at 17.5-6.

sentences.t:
युक्ताहारविहारस्य युक्तचेष्टस्य कर्मसु ।
युक्तस्वप्नावबोधस्य योगो भवति दुःखहा ॥
sentences.tr:
yukta-āhāra-vihārasya yukta-ceṣṭasya karmasu |
yukta-svapna-avabodhasya yogaḥ bhavati duḥkha-hā ||

morph.gloss: moderate, regulated (first compound member; yukta + āhāra → yuktāhāra)
food, eating (second member)
recreation, activity (yukta-āhāra-vihāra: 'whose eating and recreation are regulated', gen. sg.)
regulated (first compound member)
exertion, movement (yukta-ceṣṭa: 'whose exertion is regulated', gen. sg.)
action (loc. pl. 'in his undertakings')
regulated (first compound member)
sleep (second member; svapna + a- → svapnā-)
waking (yukta-svapna-avabodha: 'whose sleep and waking are regulated', gen. sg.)
yoga (nom. sg., subject; -aḥ before b- → -o)
to be, become (bhavati: present 3rd sg.)
sorrow, suffering (first compound member)
to destroy, remove (-hā: agent noun, duḥkha-hā 'destroyer of sorrow', nom. sg., predicate)

sentences.l: Of one regulated in eating and recreation, regulated in exertion in his undertakings, regulated in sleep and waking, yoga becomes a destroyer of sorrow.
sentences.i: For one who is moderate in eating and recreation, moderate in his efforts at work, and moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of all sorrow.
sentences.n: This states the positive counterpart to verse 16's list of extremes to avoid: yukta, "yoked, regulated, moderate", is applied in turn to eating and recreation, to effort in action, and to sleep and waking; yoga so practiced is called duḥkha-hā, "the destroyer of sorrow", the promised result of this disciplined middle way.

sentences.t:
यदा विनियतं चित्तमात्मन्येवावतिष्ठते ।
निःस्पृहः सर्वकामेभ्यो युक्त इत्युच्यते तदा ॥
sentences.tr:
yadā viniyatam cittam ātmani eva avatiṣṭhate |
niḥspṛhaḥ sarva-kāmebhyaḥ yuktaḥ iti ucyate tadā ||

morph.gloss: when
to restrain thoroughly, control (viniyata: past participle 'thoroughly restrained', nom. sg. neut., agreeing with cittam)
mind (nom. sg. neut., subject; cittam + ā- → cittamā-)
self (ātmani: loc. sg. 'in the self')
alone, only (ātmani + eva → ātmanyeva)
to stand, abide, rest (avatiṣṭhate: present middle 3rd sg. 'rests, abides')
free from longing, desireless (nom. sg.)
all (first compound member)
desire (sarva-kāma: 'all desires', abl. pl. 'from all desires'; -aḥ before y- → -o)
to yoke, join, discipline (oneself) (yukta: past participle 'disciplined', nom. sg.; -aḥ dropped before the vowel i-)
thus (iti + u- → ity u-)
to say (ucyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is called')
then

sentences.l: When the thoroughly restrained mind rests in the self alone, free of longing for all desires — then he is called disciplined.
sentences.i: When the thoroughly restrained mind rests in the self alone, free of longing for any desire, then he is called a disciplined man.
sentences.n: This defines yukta, "disciplined" (the term used repeatedly since verse 8), as the state in which the mind, fully controlled, comes to rest ātmani eva, "in the self alone" — the goal toward which the whole regimen of verses 10-17 has been aimed, illustrated next by the lamp-simile of verse 19.

sentences.t:
यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता ।
योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः ॥
sentences.tr:
yathā dīpaḥ nivāta-sthaḥ na iṅgate sā upamā smṛtā |
yoginaḥ yata-cittasya yuñjataḥ yogam ātmanaḥ ||

morph.gloss: as, just as
a lamp (nom. sg., subject; -aḥ before n- → -o)
a windless place (first compound member)
standing, situated (nivāta-stha: 'situated in a windless place', nom. sg.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
not (na + i- → ne-)
to flicker, waver (iṅgate: present middle 3rd sg. 'flickers, wavers')
that (sā: nom. sg. fem.; sā + u- → sopamā)
comparison, simile (nom. sg. fem., subject of smṛtā)
to hand down in tradition, remember (smṛtā: past participle 'traditionally held', nom. sg. fem., predicate)
a yogin (gen. sg. 'of the yogin'; -aḥ before y- → -o)
to restrain (yata: past participle, first compound member)
mind (yata-citta: 'whose mind is restrained', gen. sg.)
to yoke, join, discipline (oneself) (yuñjat: present participle 'practicing', gen. sg. 'of one practicing'; -aḥ before y- → -o)
yoga (acc. sg., object of yuñjataḥ; yogam + ā- → yogamā-)
self (ātmanaḥ: gen. sg. 'of the self')

sentences.l: As a lamp situated in a windless place does not flicker — that comparison is handed down for the yogin of restrained mind, practicing the yoga of the self.
sentences.i: As a lamp in a windless place does not flicker — that is the traditional image for the yogin of disciplined mind, practicing the yoga of the self.
sentences.n: One of the poem's most quoted images: the steadiness of a flame sheltered from wind (nivāta-sthaḥ ... na iṅgate) figures the mind of the yogin once it has come to rest, as just described in verse 18. This concrete simile completes the abstract description of a "disciplined" mind, and Śaṅkara's commentary treats it as the standard illustration (upamā smṛtā, "the traditional comparison") for one-pointed concentration.

sentences.t:
यत्रोपरमते चित्तं निरुद्धं योगसेवया ।
यत्र चैवात्मनात्मानं पश्यन्नात्मनि तुष्यति ॥
sentences.tr:
yatra uparamate cittam niruddham yoga-sevayā |
yatra ca eva ātmanā ātmānam paśyan ātmani tuṣyati ||

morph.gloss: where, in the state in which (yatra + u- → yatro-)
to cease, come to rest (uparamate: present middle 3rd sg. 'ceases, comes to rest')
mind (nom. sg. neut., subject)
to restrain, check (niruddha: past participle 'restrained, checked', nom. sg. neut., agreeing with cittam)
yoga (first compound member)
practice, application (yoga-sevā: 'the practice of yoga', instr. sg. 'through the practice of yoga')
where, in the state in which
and (ca + e- → cai-)
indeed, also
self (ātmanā: instr. sg. 'by the self')
self (ātmānam: acc. sg., object of paśyan; ātmanā + ā- → ātmanā-)
to see (paśyan: present participle 'seeing', nom. sg.; paśyan + ā- → paśyanna-)
self (ātmani: loc. sg. 'in the self')
to be satisfied, content (tuṣyati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Where the mind, restrained by the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and where, seeing the self by the self, he is content in the self,
sentences.i: The state in which the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest, and in which, seeing the self by the self, one finds contentment in the self,
sentences.n: This begins a description, continuing through verse 23, of the state attained through the practice just outlined: yoga-sevayā, "through the practice of yoga", restrains the mind until it uparamate, "ceases its wandering", and the self comes to see itself by itself (ātmanā ātmānam paśyan) — a phrase recalling verse 5's self-by-self language, now describing not moral effort but direct realization. The sentence is completed by yat tat sukham, "that happiness which...", in verse 21.

sentences.t:
सुखमात्यन्तिकं यत्तद् बुद्धिग्राह्यमतीन्द्रियम् ।
वेत्ति यत्र न चैवायं स्थितश्चलति तत्त्वतः ॥
sentences.tr:
sukham ātyantikam yat tat buddhi-grāhyam atīndriyam |
vetti yatra na ca eva ayam sthitaḥ calati tattvataḥ ||

morph.gloss: happiness (acc. sg. neut., object of vetti; sukham + ā- → sukhamā-)
absolute, ultimate, unsurpassed (acc. sg. neut., agreeing with sukham)
which (yat: nom./acc. sg. neut. relative)
that (tat: acc. sg. neut., in apposition to sukham; -t + b- → -d b-)
intellect (first compound member)
to be grasped, apprehended (gerundive of grah, buddhi-grāhya: 'graspable by the intellect [alone]', acc. sg. neut., agreeing with tat)
beyond the senses, transcending the senses (acc. sg. neut., agreeing with tat; grāhyam + a- → grāhyama-)
to know (vetti: present 3rd sg. 'he knows')
where, in the state in which
not
and (ca + e- → cai-)
indeed
this, this one (ayam: nom. sg. masc., subject of calati; eva + a- → evā-)
to stand, be established (sthita: past participle 'established', nom. sg., agreeing with ayam; -aḥ + c- → -aś c-)
to move, waver (calati: present 3rd sg.)
reality, true nature (adverbial abl. 'in reality, truly')

sentences.l: That absolute happiness which is graspable by the intellect alone, beyond the senses — he knows it, where established this one does not indeed waver, in reality.
sentences.i: He knows that supreme happiness, which is grasped by the intellect alone and lies beyond the senses; established there, he does not waver from the truth.
sentences.n: This names the content of the state described in verse 20: sukham ātyantikam, "absolute, ultimate happiness", is buddhi-grāhyam, "graspable by the intellect" and so atīndriyam, "beyond the senses" — a happiness of a wholly different order from the sense-born pleasures criticized at 5.22. Sthitaḥ ... na calati tattvataḥ, "established, he does not waver from the truth", names the stability that is the fruit of the whole meditative discipline, exemplified concretely in the next two verses.

sentences.t:
यं लब्ध्वा चापरं लाभं मन्यते नाधिकं ततः ।
यस्मिन्स्थितो न दुःखेन गुरुणापि विचाल्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
yam labdhvā ca aparam lābham manyate na adhikam tataḥ |
yasmin sthitaḥ na duḥkhena guruṇā api vicālyate ||

to obtain, gain (labdhvā: gerund 'having obtained')
and (ca + a- → cā-)
other, further (aparam: acc. sg. masc., agreeing with lābham)
gain, profit (acc. sg. masc., object of labdhvā and manyate)
to think, consider (manyate: present middle 3rd sg.)

greater, superior (adhikam: acc. sg. masc., predicate)

to stand, abide (sthita: past participle 'established', nom. sg.; -aḥ before n- → -o)
not
sorrow, suffering (instr. sg. 'by sorrow')
heavy, severe (instr. sg. 'by [something] severe')
even (guruṇā + api → guruṇāpi)
to shake, move (causative vicālyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is shaken, is moved')

sentences.l: Having gained which, he considers no other gain greater than that; established in which, he is not shaken even by heavy sorrow —
sentences.i: Having gained it, he thinks no other gain is greater; established in it, he is not shaken even by the heaviest sorrow —
sentences.n: This continues the description of the happiness named in verse 21 with two tests of its supremacy: no other gain (lābham) surpasses it, and no sorrow, however severe (guruṇā ... duḥkhena), can dislodge one established in it — a steadiness echoing verse 7's equanimity in pleasure and pain, defined by name in the next verse.

sentences.t:
तं विद्याद्दुःखसंयोगवियोगं योगसंज्ञितम् ।
स निश्चयेन योक्तव्यो योगोऽनिर्विण्णचेतसा ॥

tam vidyāt duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyogam yoga-saṃjñitam |
saḥ niścayena yoktavyaḥ yogaḥ anirviṇṇa-cetasā ||

morph.gloss: that (acc. sg. masc., object of vidyāt)

sorrow, suffering (first compound member)

yoga (first compound member)

sentences.l: That one should know as disjunction from union with sorrow, designated by the name yoga; that yoga is to be practiced resolutely, with a mind that does not despair.
sentences.i: One should know that as yoga: the severing of union with sorrow; it should be practiced with resolve and with a mind that does not grow despondent.
sentences.n: This gives the chapter's formal definition of yoga: duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyoga, "severance from union with sorrow" — a technical, almost Sāṃkhya-style phrase, comparable to the Yoga-sūtra's own opening definitions — naming the goal all the preceding practice has served. Anirviṇṇa-cetasā, "with an undespairing mind", anticipates the very despondency Arjuna will confess in verses 33-34 and 37-39, which the rest of the chapter answers.

sentences.t:
संकल्पप्रभवान्कामांस्त्यक्त्वा सर्वानशेषतः ।
मनसैवेन्द्रियग्रामं विनियम्य समन्ततः ॥
sentences.tr:
saṃkalpa-prabhavān kāmān tyaktvā sarvān aśeṣataḥ |
manasā eva indriya-grāmam viniyamya samantataḥ ||

morph.gloss: resolve, willed intention (first compound member)

desire (acc. pl., object of tyaktvā; -ān + t- → -āṃs t-)
to abandon (tyaktvā: gerund 'having abandoned')

without remainder, entirely (adverb)

alone, only (eva + indriya → evendriya-)

sentences.l: Having abandoned entirely, without remainder, the desires arising from willed resolve, and having thoroughly restrained, by the mind alone, the whole group of senses on every side,
sentences.i: Having given up entirely and without exception all desires born of willed intention, and having fully reined in, by the mind alone, the whole array of the senses on every side,
sentences.n: This begins the practical instruction, continuing through verse 26, for achieving the renunciation of saṃkalpa urged since verse 2: saṃkalpa-prabhavān kāmān, "desires arising from willed resolve", names desire's source precisely, and manasā eva, "by the mind alone", without external constraint, is the sole instrument by which the whole array of the senses (indriya-grāmam) is to be restrained — completed by the verb in verse 25.

sentences.t:
शनैः शनैरुपरमेद्बुद्ध्या धृतिगृहीतया ।
आत्मसंस्थं मनः कृत्वा न किंचिदपि चिन्तयेत् ॥
sentences.tr:
śanaiḥ śanaiḥ uparamet buddhyā dhṛti-gṛhītayā |
ātma-saṃstham manaḥ kṛtvā na kiṃcit api cintayet ||

to make (kṛtvā: gerund 'having made')

sentences.l: Little by little let him bring the mind to rest, by the intellect held firm with steadiness; having made the mind rest in the self, let him not think of anything at all.
sentences.i: Little by little let him bring the mind to rest, guided by an intellect held steady and firm; having fixed the mind so that it rests in the self, let him think of nothing else at all.
sentences.n: Śanaiḥ śanaiḥ, "slowly, slowly", doubled for emphasis, prescribes a gradual method rather than abrupt suppression; dhṛti-gṛhītayā buddhyā, "by an intellect held firm through steadiness", makes the higher faculty, buddhi, the instrument that reins in the mind, manas — a hierarchy assumed throughout the verse. Ātma-saṃstham ... na kiṃcid api cintayet, "resting in the self ... let him think of nothing at all", names the goal as a total absence of discursive thought, the same stillness pictured by the windless lamp of verse 19.

sentences.t:
यतो यतो निश्चरति मनश्चञ्चलमस्थिरम् ।
ततस्ततो नियम्यैतदात्मन्येव वशं नयेत् ॥
sentences.tr:
yataḥ yataḥ niścarati manaḥ cañcalam asthiram |
tataḥ tataḥ niyamya etat ātmani eva vaśam nayet ||

unstable, restless (nom. sg. neut., agreeing with manaḥ; cañcalam + a- → cañcalama-)

sentences.l: From whatever, from whatever cause the mind, fickle and unstable, strays forth, from there, from there let him restrain it and lead it under the control of the self alone.
sentences.i: Wherever the fickle, unsteady mind wanders off to, from there let him rein it in each time and bring it back under the control of the self.
sentences.n: Yato yataḥ ... tatas tataḥ, "from wherever ... from there", doubled on both sides, describes the repeated, patient work of the practice just prescribed: every time the mind strays it is drawn back, not corrected once and for all. Cañcalam asthiram, "fickle and unstable", is the tradition's standard description of manas, echoed by Arjuna himself in verse 34's cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ.

sentences.t:
प्रशान्तमनसं ह्येनं योगिनं सुखमुत्तमम् ।
उपैति शान्तरजसं ब्रह्मभूतमकल्मषम् ॥
sentences.tr:
praśānta-manasam hi enam yoginam sukham uttamam |
upaiti śānta-rajasam brahma-bhūtam akalmaṣam ||

sentences.l: For this yogin, of calmed mind, of quieted rajas, become brahman, stainless — supreme happiness comes to him.
sentences.i: Supreme happiness comes to this yogin, whose mind is calmed, whose rajas is stilled, who has become one with brahman, and who is free of all taint.
sentences.n: This describes the fruit of the practice completed in verses 24-26: śānta-rajasam, "whose rajas — passion, the active guṇa — is stilled", anticipates the guṇa-vocabulary made explicit from chapter 14 onward, while brahma-bhūtam, "become brahman", repeats 5.24's brahma-bhūtaḥ for one who has attained identity with brahman; sukham uttamam, "supreme happiness", names the same state as verse 21's sukham ātyantikam.

sentences.t:
युञ्जन्नेवं सदात्मानं योगी विगतकल्मषः ।
सुखेन ब्रह्मसंस्पर्शमत्यन्तं सुखमश्नुते ॥
sentences.tr:

sukhena brahma-saṃsparśam atyantam sukham aśnute ||

sentences.l: Thus always disciplining the self, the yogin, freed from taint, easily attains contact with brahman, unending happiness.
sentences.i: Thus always disciplining himself, the yogin, freed from all taint, easily attains contact with brahman, an unending happiness.
sentences.n: This repeats verse 15's opening line, yuñjann evaṃ sadātmānaṃ ... yogī, almost word for word, now naming the result as brahma-saṃsparśam, "contact with brahman" — the same attainment as verse 27's brahma-bhūtam — described here as sukham atyantam, "unending happiness", reached sukhena, "easily, without strain", once the discipline is established.

sentences.t:
सर्वभूतस्थमात्मानं सर्वभूतानि चात्मनि ।
ईक्षते योगयुक्तात्मा सर्वत्र समदर्शनः ॥

sarva-bhūta-stham ātmānam sarva-bhūtāni ca ātmani |
īkṣate yoga-yukta-ātmā sarvatra sama-darśanaḥ ||

sentences.l: The self abiding in all beings, and all beings in the self — thus he sees, whose self is disciplined by yoga, everywhere, of equal vision.
sentences.i: He whose self is disciplined by yoga sees the self abiding in all beings, and all beings abiding in the self; he sees the same everywhere.
sentences.n: This states the culminating vision of the chapter's practice: the disciplined yogin sees the self abiding in all beings and all beings abiding in the self, a mutual, reciprocal identity then applied personally to Kṛṣṇa in the next verse. Sama-darśanaḥ, "of equal vision", echoing sama-buddhiḥ in verse 9 and sama-loṣṭāśma-kāñcanaḥ in verse 8, names the culmination of equal-sightedness: not mere impartiality among classes of people, but the perception of one self in every being.

sentences.t:
यो मां पश्यति सर्वत्र सर्वं च मयि पश्यति ।
तस्याहं न प्रणश्यामि स च मे न प्रणश्यति ॥
sentences.tr:
yaḥ mām paśyati sarvatra sarvam ca mayi paśyati |
tasya aham na praṇaśyāmi saḥ ca me na praṇaśyati ||

sentences.l: Who sees me everywhere, and sees everything in me — for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to me.
sentences.i: For the man who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me, I am never lost, and he is never lost to me.
sentences.n: This applies verse 29's mutual vision — self in all beings, all beings in the self — specifically to Kṛṣṇa, the personal form the impersonal formula takes throughout this chapter (cf. verses 14-15, 31, 47). Na praṇaśyāmi ... na praṇaśyati, "I am not lost ... he is not lost", is a mutual, reciprocal bond of unfailing presence between devotee and Lord, anticipating the language of devotion at 9.31 and the promise of protection at 18.66.

sentences.t:
सर्वभूतस्थितं यो मां भजत्येकत्वमास्थितः ।
सर्वथा वर्तमानोऽपि स योगी मयि वर्तते ॥

sarva-bhūta-sthitam yaḥ mām bhajati ekatvam āsthitaḥ |
sarvathā vartamānaḥ api saḥ yogī mayi vartate ||

being (second member)

who (nom. sg. masc. relative; -aḥ before m- → -o)
I (acc. sg. 'me', object of bhajati)

sentences.l: Who, grounded in oneness, worships me abiding in all beings — that yogin, however he is engaged, dwells in me.
sentences.i: The yogin who, established in oneness, worships me as present in all beings, dwells in me, however he may be engaged.
sentences.n: Ekatvam āsthitaḥ, "grounded in oneness", names the realization of verse 29 — the self in all beings — as the basis for a devotional act, bhajati, "worships", directed at Kṛṣṇa as sarva-bhūta-sthitam, "abiding in all beings" — joining the impersonal vision of oneness to personal devotion. Sarvathā vartamānaḥ api, "however he may be engaged, in whatever way he acts", makes this dwelling-in-Kṛṣṇa independent of outward circumstance, developed further in verse 47's ranking of the devoted yogin as supreme of all.

sentences.t:
आत्मौपम्येन सर्वत्र समं पश्यति योऽर्जुन ।
सुखं वा यदि वा दुःखं स योगी परमो मतः ॥

ātma-aupamyena sarvatra samam paśyati yaḥ arjuna |
sukham vā yadi vā duḥkham saḥ yogī paramaḥ mataḥ ||

Arjuna (vocative)

sentences.l: By likeness with himself, everywhere the same he sees, whether pleasure or, if, pain, Arjuna — that yogin is held to be supreme.
sentences.i: The yogin who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere — whether it be pleasure or pain, Arjuna — is held to be supreme.
sentences.n: Ātma-aupamyena, "by likeness with oneself" — Śaṅkara explains that as one desires happiness and shuns suffering for oneself, so one should recognize the same in all beings and treat them accordingly — gives the practical method behind the equal vision of verses 29-30: reasoning from one's own case to every other. This verse closes the long meditation-and-vision teaching that opened at verse 10 and prompts Arjuna's doubting question, in verse 33, about the mind's instability.

एतस्याहं न पश्यामि चञ्चलत्वात्स्थितिं स्थिराम् ॥
sentences.tr:
yaḥ ayam yogaḥ tvayā proktaḥ sāmyena madhusūdana |
etasya aham na paśyāmi cañcalatvāt sthitim sthirām ||

this (ayam: nom. sg. masc., in apposition, 'this yoga')
yoga (nom. sg., subject; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
you (tvayā: instr. sg. 'by you')
to declare, proclaim (prokta: past participle 'declared, taught', nom. sg., predicate)
sameness, equanimity, evenness (instr. sg. 'through equanimity')
'slayer of Madhu', Kṛṣṇa (vocative)

I (nom. sg., subject of paśyāmi)

firm, steady, lasting (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with sthitim)

sentences.l: This yoga which by you has been declared, through equanimity, O slayer of Madhu — of this I do not see a steady continuance, because of fickleness.
sentences.i: Kṛṣṇa, this yoga you have taught, resting on equanimity — I cannot see how it endures steadily, because the mind is so restless.
sentences.n: Arjuna picks up sāmya, "equanimity, evenness", the very quality just praised in verses 29-32, but objects to its practicability: sthitiṃ sthirām, "a steady, lasting state", seems impossible to him given the mind's cañcalatva, "fickleness", a term he elaborates in the next verse. This objection opens a short exchange (33-36) on the mind's difficulty, structurally similar to Arjuna's earlier questions in chapter 3.

sentences.t:
चञ्चलं हि मनः कृष्ण प्रमाथि बलवद्दृढम् ।
तस्याहं निग्रहं मन्ये वायोरिव सुदुष्करम् ॥

tasya aham nigraham manye vāyoḥ iva su-duṣkaram ||

sentences.l: For the mind is fickle, Kṛṣṇa, turbulent, strong, obstinate; its restraint I consider as difficult as that of the wind, very hard to accomplish.
sentences.i: For the mind is restless, Kṛṣṇa — turbulent, powerful, and stubborn; restraining it seems to me as hard as restraining the wind.
sentences.n: Cañcalaṃ hi manaḥ throws the tradition's own description in verse 26 (cañcalam asthiram) back at Kṛṣṇa, now as an objection rather than an instruction. The wind-simile, vāyor iva su-duṣkaram, "as hard as restraining the wind", is proverbial for something ungraspable, and sets up Kṛṣṇa's answer in the next two verses.

अभ्यासेन तु कौन्तेय वैराग्येण च गृह्यते ॥

sentences.l: Without doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is hard to restrain and unsteady; but by practice, O son of Kuntī, and by dispassion, it is restrained.
sentences.i: Without doubt, mighty-armed one, the mind is unsteady and hard to control; but it can be brought under control, Kaunteya, through practice and through dispassion.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa concedes Arjuna's point entirely, asaṃśayam, "without doubt", before giving the remedy: abhyāsa, "repeated practice", and vairāgya, "dispassion" toward sense-objects — the two means the Yoga tradition, and Śaṅkara's commentary here, treat as jointly necessary and mutually reinforcing, neither sufficient alone.

sentences.t:
असंयतात्मना योगो दुष्प्राप इति मे मतिः ।
वश्यात्मना तु यतता शक्योऽवाप्तुमुपायतः ॥
sentences.tr:
asaṃyata-ātmanā yogaḥ duṣprāpaḥ iti me matiḥ |
vaśya-ātmanā tu yatatā śakyaḥ avāptum upāyataḥ ||

morph.gloss: unrestrained, uncontrolled (first compound member)
self (a-saṃyata-ātman: 'by one whose self is uncontrolled', instr. sg.)
yoga (nom. sg., subject; -aḥ before d- → -o)
hard, difficult (prefix)
to attain (prāpa: verbal adjective 'attainable'; duṣ-prāpa: 'hard to attain', nom. sg., predicate; -aḥ dropped before the vowel i-)
thus (closes the reported opinion)
I (me: enclitic gen. sg. 'my')

controllable, subject to one's will (first compound member)
self (vaśya-ātman: 'by one whose self is controlled', instr. sg.)

to be able (śakya: gerundive 'possible, able to be [attained]', nom. sg., predicate; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)

means, method (upāyataḥ: adverbial abl. 'by the [right] means')

sentences.l: By one whose self is uncontrolled, yoga is hard to attain — this is my opinion; but by one whose self is controlled, who is striving, it is possible to attain, by the right means.
sentences.i: For a man whose self is uncontrolled, yoga is hard to attain, I think; but for one who has mastered himself and strives with the right means, it is attainable.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa restates verse 35's answer in terms of two contrasted types: asaṃyatātmanā, "by one whose self is uncontrolled", for whom yoga is duṣprāpaḥ, "hard to attain", against vaśyātmanā ... yatatā, "by one whose self is controlled and who strives", for whom it is attainable upāyataḥ, "by the right means" — namely the abhyāsa and vairāgya just named. This closes Kṛṣṇa's first answer and sets up Arjuna's further, more troubled question in verses 37-39.

sentences.t: अर्जुन उवाच

sentences.l: Arjuna said

morph.gloss: Arjuna, the third Pāṇḍava, the great archer (nom. sg.)
to speak (uvāca: perfect 3rd sg. 'said')

sentences.t:
अयतिः श्रद्धयोपेतो योगाच्चलितमानसः ।
अप्राप्य योगसंसिद्धिं कां गतिं कृष्ण गच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
ayatiḥ śraddhayā upetaḥ yogāt calita-mānasaḥ |
aprāpya yoga-saṃsiddhim kām gatim kṛṣṇa gacchati ||

morph.gloss: one lacking [sufficient] effort or self-discipline, not a [successful] ascetic (nom. sg.)
faith (instr. sg. 'with faith')
to approach, be endowed with (upeta: past participle 'endowed with', nom. sg.; śraddhayā + u- → śraddhayo-; -aḥ before y- → -o)
yoga (abl. sg. 'from yoga'; yogāt + c- → yogāc c-)
to move, waver (calita: past participle 'fallen away', first compound member)
mind (calita-mānasa: 'whose mind has fallen away [from yoga]', nom. sg.)
not (negative prefix)
to attain (prāpya: gerund 'having attained'; a-prāpya: 'not having attained')
yoga (first compound member)
full accomplishment, perfection (yoga-saṃsiddhi: 'the full accomplishment of yoga', acc. sg., object of aprāpya)

Kṛṣṇa (vocative)
to go (gacchati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: One lacking effort, endowed with faith, whose mind has fallen away from yoga, not having attained the full accomplishment of yoga — what course does he go to, Kṛṣṇa?
sentences.i: Kṛṣṇa, what becomes of a man who has faith but lacks the discipline to succeed, whose mind falls away from yoga before he has attained its full accomplishment?
sentences.n: Ayatiḥ, "one lacking sufficient effort", is glossed by Śaṅkara as one who begins with śraddhā, "faith", but fails to persevere with full effort — a new worry Arjuna raises here, distinct from verse 34's doubt about the mind's fickleness in general. Yoga-saṃsiddhim, "the complete accomplishment of yoga", is the goal such a person falls short of; his fate is the question Kṛṣṇa answers at length in verses 40-45.

sentences.t:
कच्चिन्नोभयविभ्रष्टश्छिन्नाभ्रमिव नश्यति ।
अप्रतिष्ठो महाबाहो विमूढो ब्रह्मणः पथि ॥
sentences.tr:
kaccit na ubhaya-vibhraṣṭaḥ chinna-abhram iva naśyati |
apratiṣṭhaḥ mahā-bāho vimūḍhaḥ brahmaṇaḥ pathi ||

morph.gloss: is it not that? (introduces an anxious question)
not (kaccit + na → kaccinna, -t + n- → -n n-)
both (first compound member; na + u- → no-)
fallen away, ruined (past participle of vi-bhraṃś, ubhaya-vibhraṣṭa: 'fallen from both [worldly action and yoga]', nom. sg.)
to cut, sever (chinna: past participle 'torn, scattered', first compound member)
a cloud (chinna-abhra: 'a torn, scattered cloud', used adverbially in the simile)
like, as
to perish, be destroyed, vanish (naśyati: present 3rd sg.)
without support, without a footing (nom. sg.; -aḥ before m- → -o)
great (first compound member)
arm (mahā-bāhu: 'mighty-armed', vocative)
to become deluded, bewildered (vimūḍha: past participle 'bewildered', nom. sg.; -aḥ before b- → -o)
brahman, kept untranslated (gen. sg. 'toward brahman')
path, road (loc. sg. 'on the path')

sentences.l: Does he not, fallen from both, perish like a torn cloud, without a footing, mighty-armed one, bewildered on the path to brahman?
sentences.i: Does he not perish like a shredded cloud, fallen from both, with no support anywhere, bewildered on the path to brahman, mighty-armed one?
sentences.n: Kaccit, "is it not so that ...?", marks an anxious question. Ubhaya-vibhraṣṭaḥ, "fallen from both", is explained by the tradition as fallen from both the worldly path of action, which he abandoned for yoga, and the path of yoga itself, since he failed to complete it — left, like a wind-scattered cloud, with apratiṣṭhaḥ, "no footing" anywhere. Brahmaṇaḥ pathi, "on the path to brahman", names the goal such a seeker was aiming for.

sentences.t:
एतन्मे संशयं कृष्ण छेत्तुमर्हस्यशेषतः ।
त्वदन्यः संशयस्यास्य छेत्ता न ह्युपपद्यते ॥
sentences.tr:
etat me saṃśayam kṛṣṇa chettum arhasi aśeṣataḥ |
tvat anyaḥ saṃśayasya asya chettā na hi upapadyate ||

morph.gloss: this (etat: acc. sg. neut., object of chettum, referring to saṃśayam; -t + m- → -n m-)
I (me: enclitic gen. sg. 'my')
doubt (acc. sg., in apposition to etat)
Kṛṣṇa (vocative)
to cut, sever, dispel (chettum: infinitive 'to dispel')
to deserve, be fit to (arhasi: present 2nd sg. 'you should, you are fit to'; chettum + a- → chettuma-)
completely, without remainder (adverb)
you (tvat: abl. sg. 'than you')
other (anyaḥ: nom. sg., subject of upapadyate, 'someone other than you')
doubt (gen. sg. 'of this doubt')
this (asya: gen. sg., agreeing with saṃśayasya; saṃśayasya + a- → saṃśayasyā-)
to cut, dispel (chettṛ: agent noun 'a dispeller', nom. sg., predicate)
not
for, indeed (hi + u- → hyu-)
to be found, to be possible (upapadyate: present middle 3rd sg. 'is to be found, exists')

sentences.l: This my doubt, Kṛṣṇa, you should dispel completely; for other than you, a dispeller of this doubt is not to be found.
sentences.i: You must dispel this doubt of mine completely, Kṛṣṇa; for no one but you can be found to dispel it.
sentences.n: Arjuna closes his question with a direct appeal, naming Kṛṣṇa as the only possible chettā, "dispeller" — an agent noun from the same root, chid, "to cut off", as chettum in the line above — echoing the structure of similar appeals elsewhere (cf. 2.7's "I am your pupil"). Kṛṣṇa's answer, beginning in verse 40, is his longest single reply so far in this chapter.

sentences.t: श्रीभगवानुवाच
sentences.tr: śrībhagavān uvāca
sentences.l: The Blessed Lord said

the Blessed One, the Lord — Kṛṣṇa's title as speaker (nom. sg. bhagavān; -n + u- written joined)
to speak (uvāca: perfect 3rd sg. 'said')

sentences.t:
पार्थ नैवेह नामुत्र विनाशस्तस्य विद्यते ।
न हि कल्याणकृत्कश्चिद्दुर्गतिं तात गच्छति ॥
sentences.tr:
pārtha na eva iha na amutra vināśaḥ tasya vidyate |
na hi kalyāṇa-kṛt kaścit durgatim tāta gacchati ||

morph.gloss: 'son of Pṛthā', Arjuna (vocative)
not (na + e- → nai-)
indeed, at all
here, in this world (eva + i- → eve-)
not (na + a- → nā-)
there, in the world beyond
to perish, be destroyed (vināśa: noun 'destruction, ruin', nom. sg., subject; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
of him (tasya: gen. sg. 'his')
to exist, be found (vidyate: present middle 3rd sg. 'exists, is found')
not
for, indeed
good, virtuous (first compound member)
doing, one who does (kalyāṇa-kṛt: 'one who has done good', nom. sg.)
anyone (kaścit: nom. sg. 'anyone'; kṛt + kaścit written together)
an evil state, a bad end (acc. sg., object of gacchati; kaścit + d- → kaścid d-)
dear one, my son (a term of affection, vocative)
to go (gacchati: present 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: O son of Pṛthā, neither here nor there is his destruction found; for no one who does good, my dear, goes to an evil state.
sentences.i: Pārtha, no ruin awaits him, neither in this world nor the next; for no one who has done good, my son, ever comes to a bad end.
sentences.n: Kṛṣṇa opens his reassurance by flatly denying the destruction Arjuna feared in verse 38: neither iha, "here, in this life", nor amutra, "there, after death", does such a person come to ruin. Tāta, "dear one, my son", is an unusually intimate address, found only here in the poem, underscoring the warmth of the reassurance; kalyāṇa-kṛt, "one who has done good", names the yoga-practice itself, however incomplete, as a meritorious act whose fruit cannot simply vanish — the principle the next verses make concrete.

sentences.t:
प्राप्य पुण्यकृतां लोकानुषित्वा शाश्वतीः समाः ।
शुचीनां श्रीमतां गेहे योगभ्रष्टोऽभिजायते ॥
sentences.tr:
prāpya puṇya-kṛtām lokān uṣitvā śāśvatīḥ samāḥ |
śucīnām śrīmatām gehe yoga-bhraṣṭaḥ abhijāyate ||

morph.gloss: to attain, reach (prāpya: gerund 'having attained')
merit, virtue (first compound member)
doing, one who has done (puṇya-kṛt: 'one who has done meritorious deeds', gen. pl.)
world (acc. pl., object of prāpya; lokān + u- → lokānu-)
to dwell (uṣitvā: gerund 'having dwelt')
eternal, everlasting (acc. pl. fem., agreeing with samāḥ)
a year (acc. pl., object of uṣitvā: 'for [many] years')
pure, virtuous (gen. pl. 'of the pure')
prosperous, glorious (gen. pl. 'of the prosperous')
house, home (loc. sg. 'in the house')
yoga (first compound member)
fallen away (past participle of bhraṃś; yoga-bhraṣṭa: 'one fallen from yoga', nom. sg., subject; -aḥ + a- → -o with avagraha)
to be born (abhijāyate: present middle 3rd sg.)

sentences.l: Having attained the worlds of those who have done meritorious deeds, and having dwelt there for everlasting years, he who has fallen from yoga is born in the house of the pure and prosperous.
sentences.i: He who has fallen away from yoga first attains the worlds of the righteous and dwells there for countless years, and is then born again in the house of the pure and prosperous.
sentences.n: This begins Kṛṣṇa's two-stage answer to verse 38's fear: rather than perishing, the failed yogin first enjoys an afterlife among puṇya-kṛtām, "those who have done meritorious deeds" (a heavenly reward proportional to whatever merit his practice earned), then takes a new birth in the best possible circumstances, śucīnāṃ śrīmatāṃ gehe, "in the house of the pure and prosperous" — the first of two possible good rebirths, the second given in verse 42. The vulgate text translated here reads puṇyakṛtāṃ lokān uṣitvā; the BORI critical edition reads puṇyakṛtāṃl lokān uṣitvā, the final -m of puṇyakṛtām doubling the following l by sandhi, a spelling difference only, with no change in meaning.

sentences.t:
अथवा योगिनामेव कुले भवति धीमताम् ।
एतद्धि दुर्लभतरं लोके जन्म यदीदृशम् ॥
sentences.tr:
athavā yoginām eva kule bhavati dhīmatām |
etat hi durlabhataram loke janma yadi īdṛśam ||

a yogin (gen. pl. 'of yogins')
even, precisely
family, lineage (loc. sg. 'in the family')
to be, come to be (bhavati: present 3rd sg.)
wise, intelligent (gen. pl., agreeing with yoginām)
this (etat: nom. sg. neut., subject)
for, indeed (etat + hi → etaddhi)
hard to obtain, rare (comparative durlabhatara: 'rarer', nom. sg. neut., predicate)
world (loc. sg. 'in the world')
birth (nom. sg. neut., subject)
if (yadi + ī- → yadī-)
of this kind, such (nom. sg. neut., predicate agreeing with janma)

sentences.l: Or else he comes to be in the family of yogins, of the wise — for this, if of this kind, is a rarer birth in the world.
sentences.i: Or else he is born into a family of wise yogins; for a birth of this kind is harder still to obtain in this world.
sentences.n: This gives the second, still rarer good rebirth open to the fallen yogin: birth directly into a family of dhīmatām yoginām, "wise yogins", called durlabhataram, "rarer" — a comparative implying that even the śucīnāṃ śrīmatāṃ gehe of verse 41 is itself already hard to attain, and this rarer still. Together the two verses answer Arjuna's fear of total loss with its opposite: even failure in yoga leads only upward.

sentences.t:
तत्र तं बुद्धिसंयोगं लभते पौर्वदेहिकम् ।
यतते च ततो भूयः संसिद्धौ कुरुनन्दन ॥
sentences.tr:
tatra tam buddhi-saṃyogam labhate paurva-dehikam |
yatate ca tataḥ bhūyaḥ saṃsiddhau kuru-nandana ||

that (acc. sg. masc., object of labhate)
intellect, understanding (first compound member)
connection, union (buddhi-saṃyoga: 'connection with [his former] understanding', acc. sg., object of labhate)
to obtain, gain (labhate: present middle 3rd sg.)
former, prior (vṛddhi form paurva-, first compound member)
body (paurva-dehika: 'belonging to the former body', acc. sg., agreeing with buddhi-saṃyogam)
to strive, exert oneself (yatate: present middle 3rd sg.)
and
then, thereafter (-aḥ before bh- → -o)
further, more, again (comparative adverb)
full accomplishment, perfection (loc. sg. 'toward full accomplishment')
the Kuru clan (first compound member)
delighter, joy (kuru-nandana: 'joy of the Kurus', vocative, addressed to Arjuna)

sentences.l: There he regains that connection with understanding belonging to his former body, and he strives further from there toward full accomplishment, O joy of the Kurus.
sentences.i: There he recovers the understanding he had built up in his former body, and strives on from there, further still, toward complete accomplishment, joy of the Kurus.
sentences.n: Buddhi-saṃyogam paurva-dehikam, "the connection with understanding belonging to his former body", explains how progress carries over between births: the new birth, in either of verses 41-42's forms, comes with the accumulated insight of the previous life's practice already intact, so effort resumes rather than starting over — the mechanism behind the promise that nothing is lost, first stated in verse 40.

sentences.t:
पूर्वाभ्यासेन तेनैव ह्रियते ह्यवशोऽपि सः ।
जिज्ञासुरपि योगस्य शब्दब्रह्मातिवर्तते ॥

practice, repeated exercise (pūrva-abhyāsa: 'former practice', instr. sg. 'by his former practice')

precisely, alone (tena + eva → tenaiva)
to carry, draw (hriyate: present passive 3rd sg. 'is drawn, is carried along')

even, although
he (nom. sg. masc., subject)

yoga (gen. sg. 'about yoga', object of jijñāsuḥ)

sentences.l: By that very former practice, he is drawn on, even against his will; even one who merely desires to know of yoga transcends the brahman revealed in word.
sentences.i: By the strength of his former practice alone he is carried onward, even without meaning to; even one who merely wishes to learn about yoga goes beyond the brahman of the scriptures.
sentences.n: Tena eva, "by that alone", names pūrvābhyāsa, "former practice", as a force strong enough to carry a person forward hi avaśaḥ api, "even involuntarily" — practice leaves a residue independent of present will, a claim close to the later Yoga tradition's doctrine of saṃskāra. Śabda-brahma, "the brahman that consists in words", i.e. the verbal revelation of the Veda and its ritual portion, is here surpassed even by a mere jijñāsuḥ, "one desiring to know about yoga" — a striking ranking of yogic aspiration above scriptural learning, comparable to 2.46's simile of the many wells beside one great reservoir.

sentences.t:
प्रयत्नाद्यतमानस्तु योगी संशुद्धकिल्बिषः ।
अनेकजन्मसंसिद्धस्ततो याति परां गतिम् ॥
sentences.tr:

aneka-janma-saṃsiddhaḥ tataḥ yāti parām gatim ||

but, and
a yogin (nom. sg., in apposition to yatamānaḥ)
thoroughly purified (past participle, first compound member)

not one, many (first compound member)
birth (aneka-janma: 'many births', second member)
fully accomplished, perfected (past participle, aneka-janma-saṃsiddha: 'perfected through many births', nom. sg.; -aḥ + t- → -as t-)
then, thereafter (-aḥ before y- → -o)
to go (yāti: present 3rd sg.)
highest, supreme (acc. sg. fem., agreeing with gatim)
course, goal, destination (acc. sg., object of yāti)

sentences.l: But the yogin striving through effort, his sins thoroughly purified, perfected through many births, then goes to the highest goal.
sentences.i: But the yogin who strives with effort, his sins fully purified, having been perfected through many births, at last attains the highest goal.
sentences.n: This resolves the whole sequence begun at verse 37: even the yogin who fails and is reborn, as described in verses 41-43, eventually becomes a yogin whose sins are purified through repeated striving across aneka-janma, "many births", and reaches parāṃ gatim, "the highest goal", liberation itself. This closes the answer to Arjuna's question with an unambiguous assurance that no effort in yoga is ever ultimately wasted.

sentences.t:
तपस्विभ्योऽधिको योगी ज्ञानिभ्योऽपि मतोऽधिकः ।
कर्मिभ्यश्चाधिको योगी तस्माद्योगी भवार्जुन ॥

Arjuna (vocative)

sentences.l: Superior to ascetics is the yogin, held superior even to men of knowledge; superior to performers of action is the yogin — therefore be a yogin, Arjuna.
sentences.i: The yogin ranks higher than ascetics, and is held higher even than men of learning; he ranks higher than those who perform ritual acts — therefore, Arjuna, be a yogin.
sentences.n: This ranks the yogin above three other recognized types: the tapasvin, "ascetic", who practices austerity; the jñānin, "man of knowledge", who pursues theoretical understanding; and the karmin, "performer of ritual action", who follows the Vedic sacrificial path. The direct imperative, tasmād yogī bhava arjuna, "therefore be a yogin, Arjuna", is Kṛṣṇa's personal charge closing the ranking, specified in the final verse as devotion in particular.

sentences.l: And of all yogins too, he who, with inner self directed to me, full of faith, worships me — he is held by me to be the most disciplined.
sentences.i: And of all yogins, the one who, filled with faith and his inmost self fixed on me, worships me — him I hold to be the most disciplined of all.
sentences.n: The chapter's closing verse names the standard against which even the ranking of verse 46 is measured: mad-gatena antar-ātmanā, "with the inner self directed toward me", and śraddhāvān ... bhajate, "full of faith, worships", single out bhakti, personal devotion, as the culmination of the whole path of self-restraint the chapter has taught, echoing verses 30-31's bond between devotee and Kṛṣṇa. Yuktatamaḥ, "most disciplined" — a superlative of the yukta used throughout the chapter since verse 8 — closes Ātmasaṃyamayoga by ranking the devotee above every other kind of yogin, and prepares the ground on which chapter 7 opens.

about: Chapter 6, Ātmasaṃyamayoga, "the yoga of self-restraint," is the Gītā's fullest manual of meditation. It opens by redefining renunciation and yoga as one and the same thing — not abstention from the sacrificial fire or from action, but performing one's duty without attachment to its fruit — and pictures the self as either one's best friend or one's worst enemy, depending on whether it has been mastered. From there Kṛṣṇa gives concrete instructions: a solitary, moderate life; a firm seat of cloth, hide, and kuśa-grass, neither too high nor too low; an erect, motionless posture with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose; and a mind drawn back, again and again, patiently, whenever it wanders, until it rests in the self alone, as steady as a lamp in a windless place. The state this practice reaches is described first as an equal vision that sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, then, more personally, as a bond in which Kṛṣṇa is never lost to the one who sees him everywhere. Arjuna objects that the mind is as hard to hold as the wind, and then asks what becomes of a practitioner who has faith but fails to complete the discipline before death. Kṛṣṇa answers that no effort on this path is ever wasted: such a person is reborn into circumstances that let him resume his practice from where he left off, and, striving across many lifetimes if need be, eventually reaches the highest goal. The chapter closes by ranking the yogin above the ascetic, the man of mere learning, and the ritual performer alike, and above all other yogins by naming the one whose inmost self is fixed on Kṛṣṇa in faith and devotion as the most disciplined of all.
